title: MA9-06715
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXX XXXXX, a citizen of Saint Lucia, claims refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1)(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
The claimant was born in XXXXX, Saint Lucia, on XXXXX 1984.
When she was 15 years ago, she met a young man by the name of XXXXX and soon thereafter, they were living together as man and wife.
Within a few months, he became physically abusive to her. On one occasion, he stabbed her with scissors. She left the house and returned to her mother's home.
The next day, XXXXX called her and said he was sorry for what happened and promised he would mend his ways. She returned to live with him.
The abuse continued however. She cut her foot in the dark when she stepped on some glass that XXXXX had intentionally placed on the mattress on the floor.

She was treated at the hospital for her injuries. That same night, she went to the police with her mother and made a complaint against XXXXX. He was arrested, convicted and sentenced to a $250.00 fine.

XXXXX called her again. He apologized and asked her to return to him. When he came to pick her up in his car, he took her to a friend's place in the woods and threatened to kill her if she tried to leave.
The claimant was able to escape by calling her mother who came with the claimant's brother and other persons to the house and took her away.
XXXXX began to stalk her and sent messages that she was going to pay because she made him go to jail.
The claimant was afraid that XXXXX would eventually hurt her. Her mother called a friend in Toronto who sent a plane ticket to the claimant.
She left Saint Lucia by plane on XXXXX, 2002 and arrived in Toronto the same day.
She lived in Toronto until she moved to Ottawa in XXXXX, 2004, to live with her aunt XXXXX.
She alleges that she did not make a refugee claim because her aunt did not suggest that she do so.

In 2007, she started a relationship with XXXXX XXXXX who was a Canadian citizen. They began to live together in XXXXX, 2007. They wanted to marry and have XXXXX sponsor her. Unfortunately, XXXXX was murdered on XXXXX, 2009.

The claimant alleges that she did not know what to do. She was so sad and so worried about her status in Canada. Over the years, she heard from her friends and her family in Saint Lucia that XXXXX has continued to tell people that he will kill her if she returns to Saint Lucia stating that she ruined his reputation and that she was going to pay for what she did to him.
She made a refugee claim on May 1, 2009, when advised to do so by XXXXX sister. ANALYSIS Identity (as to nationality)
A certified copy of the claimant's Saint Lucia passport was presented as evidence at the hearing before me on June 28, 2010.
I find that she is a citizen of Saint Lucia. Credibility

The claimant's oral testimony was consistent with the allegations in her Personal Information Form (PIF) narrative (Exhibit C-1) and with the information she gave to the Immigration officer when she made her refugee claim on May 1, 2009. (Ex A-2)

Her father left the family home when the claimant was only four years old. Her mother married her step-father, XXXXX XXXXX, the following year. He was a violent man who beat her mother regularly and who sexually assaulted the claimant and her sister causing her sister XXXXX to leave home when she was 17 years old.

The claimant lived with her grandmother when she was 15 at a time when her mother was working in Martinique. The claimant was looking for someone to love and for support, and that is when she took up with her boyfriend XXXXX whose real name is XXXXX XXXXX
XXXXX was arrested by the Royal Saint Lucia Police Force on XXXXX, 2002, for the incident which occurred on XXXXX, 2002.
A copy of the police report dated XXXXX, 2007, confirming his arrest and a fine of $250.00 was produced into evidence (Exhibit C-3)
A copy of a report in the XXXXX Newspaper on XXXXX, 2009 referring to the stabbing death of XXXXX XXXXX in XXXXX, Quebec, was also filed into evidence (Exhibit C-4).
Also produced into evidence were two letters from the claimant's sister, XXXXX, one which is dated XXXXX 2010, and the other which is undated.
The undated letter states that she was informed that XXXXX was asking about her whereabouts.
The second letter states that she heard rumors that he XXXXX has been asking and searching for her.
The determinative issue in this case is whether Saint Lucia is able and willing to provide protection to the claimant.

The evidence before me indicates that the Saint Lucia police did provide protection to her when she asked for it following the altercation which occurred on XXXXX, 2002. The police arrested and charged XXXXX on XXXXX, 2002. He apparently appeared before a Judge and was assessed a fine of $250.00. The claimant was not called to give evidence so it would seem that XXXXX must have pleaded guilty to that charge.

Except in situations where the state is a state of complete breakdown, states must be presumed capable of protecting its citizens. This presumption can be rebutted by the claimant by "clear and convincing" evidence of Saint Lucia's inability to protect1.
The standard of protection that a country needs to offer its citizens is "--- adequate though not necessarily perfect."2

The adequacy of state protection cannot rest on the subjective fear of the claimant. Purely subjective view of the adequacy of Saint Lucia's state protection is not "direct, relevant and compelling" evidence of the inadequacy of state protection3.

The burden of proof to establish the absence of state protection is "directly proportional to the level of democracy in the state in question. The more democratic the state's institutions, the more the claimant must have done to exhaust all the courses of action open to her or him4.

Saint Lucia is a multiparty, parliamentary democracy with a population of approximately 171,000. While the government generally respected the human rights of its citizens, there were problems in a few areas including "--- violence against women, and child abuse"5.

In her submissions, counsel for the claimant, Ms. Setzer, referred to the decision of Mr. Justice Shore in the case of Mauricette v. Minister of Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness, 2008 F.C. 420, dated April 3, 2008.

The Honorable Mr. Justice Shore when dealing with the issue of state protection for victims of domestic abuse in Saint Lucia made reference to a January 6, 2006 Response to Information Request (RIR) and the fact that the Family Court magistrate can issue protection orders and the victims has to initiate the proceedings by approaching one of the social workers. The Learned Judge states further -- "It is noteworthy that the limited measures available to women to combat intimate partner violence is through family law proceedings rather than criminal law proceedings. - (Emphasis added)

The Judge continued by stating that this fact speaks to the way that violence against women is viewed by the authorities. The protection orders cited in the report focussed on prohibiting an abuser from remaining in the household residence of the victim. These would not apply to the Applicant as she has already separated from her ex-partner. "None of the protection orders address stalking behaviour." - (Emphasis added)
The Learned Judge concluded his findings on the state protection issue by stating "the documentary evidence indicates clearly that the protection available to her would be inadequate."

However, on July 13, 2009, the UNHCR published a report on domestic violence against women which dealt with legislation, family court, police services and statistics on gender-based violence and support services (2006-July 2009) for Saint Lucia prepared by the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada - citation LCA 103195.E (Exhibit A-3).
The report indicates that domestic violence is still a serious problem in Saint Lucia.

The same report states that in December, 2004, the government announced that an amended Criminal Code would take effect on January 1, 2005. The new Code contains a number of provisions that address violence against women, including the introduction of "marital rape" as an offence, as well as provisions that address stalking and workplace sexual harassment. (emphasis added) Under the amended Code, convicted rapists may face life imprisonment and unlawful sexual connection can attract a penalty of fourteen years in prison.

The Domestic Violence (Summary Proceedings) Act was passed in Saint Lucia in 1995 and allows victims of domestic abuse to seek protection, occupation and/or tenancy orders. According to the law, a protection order may prohibit the person against whom an order is issued from entering the applicant's household residence, place of work and/or place of education.

The protection, occupation and tenancy orders are issued by the magistrate at family court and are usually issued the same day that the request is made. An Attorney in St. Lucia corroborated that the family court provides "immediate assistance" to victims. According to the Attorney, the police are empowered to arrest the offender if he or she does not comply with a protection order and the police take protection orders seriously.

The family court tries cases of domestic violence and crimes against women and children. The court also employs full-time social workers to help victims of domestic violence and offers group sessions and counseling. There are two offices for the family court; one in Castries (where the claimant XXXXX) and one in Vieux Fort.

The Royal Saint Lucia Police Force (RSLPF) launched the Vulnerable Persons' Team (VPT) in December 2007 to handle all child abuse investigations and to oversee and provide advice for domestic abuse cases in Saint Lucia. All domestic violence cases are reported to the VPT corporal to ensure that they are dealt with appropriately. According to Country Reports for 2008, the VPT "increased police responsiveness" to cases involving violence against women and children, and, in the first half of 2008, there was a 24 percent increase in the number of sexual crimes reported to the police that were committed against women and children.

The Director of the Ministry of Home Affairs and Gender Relations stated that police response to domestic violence "improved significantly" in the last eight to nine years because of sensitization training provided by the Division of Gender Relations and that the improvement has been "even more noticeable" with the establishment of the VPT.

In contrast, the Executive Director of the Saint Lucia Crisis Centre (SLCC) --- did not think that the police were effective in combating domestic violence or that the formation of the VPT had improved the situation ---because several clients of the Crisis Centre reported not receiving an "appropriate response" from the police. This information could not be corroborated among the sources consulted by the Research Directorate. However, according to the Attorney, the police do not always take domestic violence cases seriously because many victims withdraw their cases.

Insofar as the support services are concerned, the Women's Support Centre, which opened in 2001 and is funded by the Saint Lucia government, provides a shelter, counseling, crisis intervention, protection planning, children's programs, public education and other assistance to victims of domestic violence -- and also runs a 24-hour hotline which offers counseling and advice. The shelter has space to accommodate a total of 25 people, including both women and children --- and it is reported that no clients are forced to leave the shelter if they do not have safe alternative housing.

When the claimant's attention was directed to the contents of this report and to the number of services available to women of domestic abuse in Saint Lucia by the family court, the police and the Women Support Centre, she acknowledged that she was not aware that such services were in existence in Saint Lucia.

No government that makes any claim to democratic values or protection of human rights can guarantee the protection of all of its citizens at all times. Where a state (like Saint Lucia) is in effective control of its territory, has military, police and civil authority in place and makes serious efforts to protect its citizens, the mere fact that it is not always successful at doing so will not be enough to justify a claim that victims of terrorism or other crimes are unable to avail themselves of such protection. (See the case of Villafranca - SUPRA.)

I find from all of the evidence that Saint Lucia is making serious efforts to protect its citizens in domestic violence cases. On the one occasion when the claimant and her mother approached the Royal Saint Lucia Police Force in XXXXX, 2002, the perpetrator of the abuse XXXXX was arrested, charged and convicted and was assessed a fine by the First District Court at Anse La Raye. (Exhibit C-3)

I find from all of the evidence that there are effective Criminal Code provisions in place in Saint Lucia to ensure the protection of domestic abuse victims such as the claimant from persons like XXXXX and that the police properly deal with the perpetrators if and when the victims of those crimes request assistance, as was done in this case.
I find from all of the evidence that the claimant has failed to present "clear and convincing" proof of Saint Lucia's inability to protect her.
In arriving at my decision, I have also taken into consideration the Chairperson's Guidelines 4 on Women Refugee Claimants Facing Gender-Related Persecution.

Having considered all of the evidence, the submissions of counsel for the claimant and having regard to the findings made with respect to the issue of state protection, I determine that the claimant has not satisfied her burden of establishing a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground or that it is more likely than not she would face a risk to her life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment upon return to Saint Lucia.
For these reasons, I find that the claimant is not a "Convention refugee" under section 96 of IRPA, or "a person in need of protection" within the meaning of section 97(1)(b) of IRPA.

Therefore, the claim of XXXXX XXXXX is rejected.
